1. Assessing the complexity of mesoscopic complex systems

The prediction of future data from sampled data is a fundamental task in science and technology [1, 2]. Unfortunately, the determination of a system’s exact dynamical equations from data is generally not possible [3], although for examples from relatively simple system classes, occasionally suitable approximations can be elaborated [4–6]. Since the discovery of universality classes [7–10], one preferred approach has therefore been to determine the system’s position in the space of systems, from which we derive a qualitative idea of how it will behave. Traditional criteria along which we structure this space are stability of the emerging dynamics and topological properties of the generated phase space. Given dynamical equations, the algorithms required for this classification (Lyapunov exponents, entropies, fractal dimensions [10–16] and distributions thereof [15–17]), have become standard.

If only measured data is available, the success of this endeavor depends critically on the description level that systems and observers require: Microscopic physics does not easily transform into macroscopy, and macroscopic descriptions lack a straightforward connection to the microscopic world. In both cases, arriving at the desired classification is nontrivial, but generally achievable. At the ‘mesoscopic’ scale between—a focus of present research—we deal, however, with an elevated problem level, brought about by inherently complex subsystems that interact in various and variable ways. Spatiotemporal chaos [18] and biological neural networks [3] are two prominent examples where it is generally unclear what the different parts contribute to the overall behavior, and how boundaries should be drawn to reliably predict a system’s behavior. Moreover, these systems tend to operate along particularly complex [19] paradigms, such as ‘life at the edge of chaos’ [20], cases for which the classical approaches, focusing on exponential information decay, were not designed. Often the hope is that the situation may be mended by using big data, but such conditions lead to exceeding computational load and to results that are often unreliable and difficult to interpret.

To overcome these difficulties, we follow an alternative path. Instead of metric data, we look at data composed of symbols, a natural setting in many experimental situations (see figure 1 and our final real-world example). Given strings of symbols, we may ask what type of ‘formal grammar’ or ‘formal language’ would be required to efficiently generate ‘similar’ data, an approach that has been fruitful in computer science for compiler design, and in automata theory [21–23]. Formal languages are naturally organized along a hierarchy of expression strength originally described by Chomsky [24]. Resolving from a string of symbols its generator or location within this hierarchy, is again impossible, as any given string can be generated by a specifically designed lower-class automaton [22]. Fortunately, the challenge can be solved in probabilistic terms. For this, we switch from individual strings to ensembles of strings, similarly to the change from classical to chaotic dynamics. Using the probabilistic concept of walk-through entropy, we showed [25] that a chosen string of symbols can indeed be associated probabilistically with a specific class in the hierarchy (lower expression strength systems may generate the same string, but only at significantly reduced probability). To enable the comparison of data of distinct sizes and to highlight the statistical physics origin, we recently refined this concept toward the notion of excess entropy [3].

Here, we demonstrate that excess entropies are an excellent tool for (1) comfortably quantifying the complexity of both data- and equation-defined systems, (2) for measuring how similar experimental data are, and (3) for assessing how well models reflect the properties of their targets. We start by formulating the relevant fundamental properties of excess entropies in mathematical language. Constructed data provide first application guidelines, whereupon the application to developing neuronal cultures illustrates how signals from sensors naturally convert into symbols (without using, e.g. ‘spike-sorting’), how excess entropy applied to the symbols provide deeper insight into high-dimensional complex real-world systems (where we may or may not use ‘big data’), and how this guides toward modeling perfection.
